assertions.text: markshust/hcf is mentioned in this evidence.
There is deliberately no 'execution' hook; the implementation loop is already covered by the pre/post-implementation and pre/post-batch hooks, so an execution hook would only duplicate them.
Running HCF requires the Claude Code CLI, a Git repository, and a test framework configured in the project.
Only devils-advocate is enrolled by default (at post-plan); standards-enforcer ships with its enrollment commented out and can be enabled by uncommenting its phase key.

Discovery failures are treated as hard errors (exit 3 for invalid phase/mode, exit 4 for mid-run enrollment change) rather than empty hooks, reflecting a design preference for failing loudly over silently running a different pipeline.
A malformed plansDir value (absolute path, .. segment, or empty string) stops the run rather than falling back to the default plans directory, and the resolver avoids a jq dependency.
Repository development practice: the plugin can be tested locally without publishing using claude --plugin-dir /path/to/hcf, with skills namespaced as /hcf:skill-name and debug output via --debug.
Plans default to .claude/plans/ but a project can set a relative plansDir in an optional .claude/hcf.json; no skill creates or modifies that file, and project-update only validates it if present.
The pipeline uses convention over configuration: there is no central registry, and each agent enrolls itself by declaring a phase, order, and mode in its own YAML frontmatter.

Run state such as task statuses, requirement checkboxes, and retry counts lives in the plan files, so an interrupted run resumes by re-running the plan; terminal outputs are ALL_TASKS_COMPLETE or TASKS_BLOCKED.
HCF does not migrate plan folders when the plans directory changes; the user must move them, and project-update warns if .claude/plans still holds plan folders after a move.
HCF separates planning (human-in-the-loop, where human and AI collaborate on requirements) from execution (fully autonomous parallel TDD implementation).

Repository development practice: contributors fork, create a feature branch, test locally with --plugin-dir, add a CHANGELOG [Unreleased] entry for user-visible changes, and submit a pull request; the repo's own test suite runs via ./tests/run-tests.sh with no dependencies beyond bash/awk/sed/sort/grep.

Skills are invocable as slash commands (/project-setup, /plan-create, /plan-orchestrate) and can also auto-trigger when a user request matches their description; project-setup and project-update are manual-invocation only.
plan-orchestrate builds batches from the task dependency graph and runs independent tasks in parallel workers, so many tasks complete in a handful of batches rather than sequentially.

The plugin ships three agents (devils-advocate, tdd-worker, standards-enforcer), four skills (project-setup, project-update, plan-create, plan-orchestrate), and hook scripts including discover-hooks.sh and gate scripts.

Discovery failures are treated as hard errors (exit 3 for invalid phase/mode, exit 4 for mid-run enrollment change) rather than empty hooks, reflecting a design preference for failing loudly over silently running a different pipeline.
A malformed plansDir value (absolute path, .. segment, or empty string) stops the run rather than falling back to the default plans directory, and the resolver avoids a jq dependency.
HCF does not migrate plan folders when the plans directory changes; the user must move them, and project-update warns if .claude/plans still holds plan folders after a move.
